book.title: SPATAIL General Science & Technology Reader
book.subtitle: Read → Select → Show in SPATAIL → interactive XR explanation
book.academicBasis: General-science basis: CK-12 FlexBooks (life / physical / earth-space science, CC BY-NC) and OpenStax (Biology, University Physics, Astronomy, Chemistry; openstax.org, CC BY). Summaries here are original paraphrases written for the demo, not redistributed verbatim.

concepts.title: Photosynthesis
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how plants transform light energy into chemical energy.
concepts.body:
Photosynthesis is the process plants use to convert light energy into stored chemical energy. In a simplified explanation, sunlight reaches the leaf, water enters through the roots, and carbon dioxide enters through small openings in the leaf. Inside chloroplasts, the plant uses these inputs to form glucose and release oxygen.

A good spatial explanation should not only show a plant. It should show the flow of matter and energy: inputs moving toward the leaf and outputs leaving it. This makes the invisible chemical process easier to understand in space.
experienceBeats: Show the leaf as the main object
Reveal sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide as inputs
Animate the chloroplast as the conversion point
Show glucose and oxygen leaving as outputs
Tap each input or output for a short explanation

concepts.title: Cell Division
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how one parent cell becomes two daughter cells.
concepts.body:
Cell division is the process by which one parent cell divides into two daughter cells. Before division is complete, the cell must copy its genetic material so each new cell receives the information it needs. The cell then separates its contents and forms two cells.

The best spatial representation is a timeline that the learner can scrub. Each stage should be visible as a beat: parent cell, DNA copying, separation, and two daughter cells. This is stronger than a static cell model because division is a process, not just an object.
experienceBeats: Show one parent cell
Highlight the nucleus and DNA
Animate DNA copying
Show the cell membrane pinching inward
End with two daughter cells and labels

concepts.title: Gravity
concepts.learningGoal: Show why unsupported objects accelerate downward near Earth.
concepts.body:
Gravity pulls objects toward Earth because Earth has mass and attracts nearby objects. When an object like an apple is unsupported, gravity causes it to accelerate downward. The apple does not move because it wants to go down; it moves because a force acts on it.

A spatial scene should make the invisible force visible. The apple, Earth, ground, and a force arrow are enough for the first version. Later, SPATAIL can add a path trail, a velocity arrow, and a comparison mode showing different planets.
experienceBeats: Place an apple above the ground
Draw a force arrow toward Earth
Animate the apple falling
Compare weak and strong gravity arrows
Reset and replay the fall

concepts.title: V8 Engine
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how pistons, connecting rods, and crankshaft motion work together.
concepts.body:
A V8 engine has eight cylinders arranged in two banks, often forming a V shape. Inside the cylinders, pistons move up and down. Connecting rods transfer this motion to the crankshaft, which rotates and sends mechanical power to the drivetrain.

The educational goal is not to create a perfect engine model. The goal is to show hidden internal relationships. A cutaway or exploded view helps the learner understand parts that are normally hidden by the engine block.
experienceBeats: Show the complete engine shape first
Fade the outer shell into a cutaway
Highlight pistons in the cylinder banks
Animate reciprocating piston motion
Show crankshaft rotation and firing sequence

concepts.title: Solar System
concepts.learningGoal: Compare the Sun and planets while preserving conceptual relationships.
concepts.body:
The solar system contains the Sun, planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and other objects held together by gravity. The planets orbit the Sun at very different distances. A perfectly accurate scale model would be too large for most rooms.

For XR, the best first representation is a compressed scale comparison. It should communicate order, relative size, and orbital relationships without pretending that the distances are fully accurate.
experienceBeats: Place the Sun as the anchor object
Arrange planets outward in order
Use compressed spacing so the scene fits the room
Show orbit rings or trails
Tap planets for size and distance facts

concepts.title: Roman Colosseum
concepts.learningGoal: Explain the structure as a layered architectural and historical space.
concepts.body:
The Roman Colosseum was a large amphitheater in ancient Rome. Its layered seating, repeated arches, internal passages, and arena floor made it a complex public structure. Understanding it spatially requires more than viewing the outside.

A good SPATAIL scene should combine a miniature overview with a cutaway. The learner can first understand the full shape, then inspect layers and movement paths inside the structure.
experienceBeats: Show a tabletop miniature of the Colosseum
Slice a section open to reveal seating layers
Highlight arches and circulation paths
Animate crowds moving through entrances
Allow a life-size section expansion for scale

concepts.title: Bridge Construction
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how a bridge is assembled from foundations to deck and cables.
concepts.body:
Bridge construction is a sequence of structural steps. Builders must create stable foundations, raise supports, connect load-bearing members, and add the deck. Different bridge types use different strategies, but all must transfer loads safely to the ground.

The best SPATAIL representation is an assembly sequence. Instead of showing a completed bridge only, the app should build the bridge in stages and show how forces travel through the structure.
experienceBeats: Start with foundations and piers
Add towers or supports
Connect cables or trusses
Place deck sections step by step
Highlight load paths through the structure

concepts.title: The Human Heart
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how the heart pumps blood through the body.
concepts.body:
The heart is a muscular pump that pushes blood through the body. Its chambers fill and contract in a steady rhythm, sending oxygen-rich blood out to the tissues and returning oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

A spatial explanation should show the beating cycle and the direction of blood flow, not just a static organ.
experienceBeats: Show the heart at rest
Highlight the four chambers
Animate one heartbeat
Show blood flowing in and out
Label the path to the lungs and body

concepts.title: DNA
concepts.learningGoal: Show how DNA stores genetic information in a double helix.
concepts.body:
DNA is a long molecule shaped like a twisted ladder — the double helix. Its rungs are pairs of chemical bases whose order spells out the instructions a cell uses to build proteins.

A spatial model can unwind the helix to reveal the base pairs, then show how the sequence carries information.
experienceBeats: Show the twisted double helix
Slow the twist to a ladder
Highlight one base pair
Reveal the sequence as information
Re-coil the helix

concepts.title: The Atom
concepts.learningGoal: Explain that atoms have a dense nucleus surrounded by electrons.
concepts.body:
An atom is the smallest unit of an element. It has a tiny, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by far lighter electrons that occupy regions around it.

Because atoms are invisibly small, scaling one up to room size lets a learner see the nucleus and the electron regions in proportion.
experienceBeats: Place the nucleus at the center
Add electrons in shells around it
Animate electrons moving
Compare the tiny nucleus to the whole atom
Label protons, neutrons, and electrons

concepts.title: The Lever
concepts.learningGoal: Show how a lever multiplies force around a fulcrum.
concepts.body:
A lever is a stiff bar that pivots on a fulcrum. Pushing down on one end lifts a load on the other, and moving the fulcrum changes how much force is needed.

A spatial scene should let the learner move the fulcrum and feel how effort and load trade off.
experienceBeats: Place a bar on a fulcrum
Add a load on one end
Push the other end to lift it
Move the fulcrum and compare effort
Show the force arrows

concepts.title: Gears
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how meshing gears change speed and turning force.
concepts.body:
Gears are toothed wheels that mesh so one turns another. A small gear driving a large gear turns slower but with more force; the sizes set the gear ratio.

A spatial scene should animate the meshing teeth and show how speed and force trade off between gears.
experienceBeats: Show two meshing gears
Animate them turning together
Highlight the meshing teeth
Compare a small and a large gear
Show the speed-versus-force trade

concepts.title: The Pendulum
concepts.learningGoal: Show why a pendulum swings back and forth at a steady period.
concepts.body:
A pendulum is a weight hung so it can swing freely. Gravity pulls it back toward the center, so it swings past and returns, keeping a steady rhythm set mostly by its length.

A spatial scene should animate the swing and show the restoring pull at each point.
experienceBeats: Hang the weight at rest
Lift it to one side
Release and animate the swing
Show the restoring force
Compare a short and a long pendulum

concepts.title: Moon Phases
concepts.learningGoal: Explain why the Moon shows different phases from Earth.
concepts.body:
The Moon does not make its own light; we see the half lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth, we view that lit half from changing angles, so it appears to grow and shrink through its phases.

A spatial scene should place the Sun, Earth, and Moon and animate the orbit to show why the lit fraction changes.
experienceBeats: Place Earth with the Moon in orbit
Light the Moon from the Sun's side
Animate the Moon around Earth
Show the phase seen from Earth at each step
Label new, quarter, and full moon

concepts.title: Skyscrapers
concepts.learningGoal: Explain how a steel frame lets a tall building stand and carry loads.
concepts.body:
A skyscraper stands on a steel (or concrete) frame of columns and beams that carries its weight down to deep foundations. The frame also resists wind, which pushes harder the higher you go.

A spatial scene should build the frame floor by floor and show how loads travel down the columns.
experienceBeats: Lay the foundation
Raise the steel columns
Add floor beams and slabs
Stack floors upward
Show loads traveling down to the ground
